messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

For nearly forty years, Meena Patel had been the person in her family who stayed calm in emergencies. At 66, she still worked nights as a security guard in a downtown office building, priding herself on noticing what others missed. That sense of vigilance shattered two years ago when her adult son was killed in a car crash. He had called her shortly before driving home, and they had ended the conversation tensely after a small disagreement about whether he was too tired to be on the road. Hours later, police told her his car had been hit at an intersection. Since then, what has tormented Meena most is not only that he died, but the conviction that she should have protected him and failed. She had come to believe that if she had insisted harder, if she had not let the call end that way, the accident would not have happened. In her mind, the event happened because of the way she acted, and from that belief grew another, darker one: that something in her had been permanently damaged, that she would never feel normal emotion again.

Those meanings attached themselves quickly to the memory itself. When Meena speaks about the crash, she does not describe it as something she learned afterward; she experiences it as if she is there, seeing twisted metal and impact in a way that feels more real than ordinary memory. If she tries to picture her son as he was before, the image is thin and distant, but the crash scene comes with punishing clarity and a force that overwhelms her so completely she has to stop talking. After one of these vivid returns, she finds traces of it everywhere, noticing damaged bumpers, traffic reports, or even a brief mention of an intersection with a sharpened attention she never had before, as though the memory itself has tuned her to scan for anything that resembles it. Each return of the memory seems to prove to her that she is the kind of mother who failed at the one moment protection mattered, and the more she thinks this, the more readily her mind seizes on any mention of accidents, any glimpse of cars hit on the roadside, as if the world is constantly presenting her with evidence of her failure. Because she had come to read herself as responsible and irreparably changed, reminders she once would have barely registered now caught hard on her attention; a roadside fender bender or a passing comment about traffic no longer felt incidental, but charged with accusation and threat. The belief that she had caused an irreversible loss meant ordinary details no longer stayed ordinary: an intersection, a tired-sounding voice on the phone, even a brief pause before someone answered became the kinds of things her mind now tagged as warnings. In that way, her own conclusions about herself and the world were helping generate the very reminders that kept finding her.

In the months after his death, Meena began organizing her life around not setting off that chain. If relatives started discussing traffic accidents, she found reasons to leave the room. She stopped attending funerals and refused to go to the cemetery with her husband on religious observances, telling herself she could not bear “all that grief.” When those reminders caught her off guard, Meena moved quickly to shut them down: she would leave family gatherings early, change the subject, or keep herself busy with tasks because staying put felt like inviting the crash back into the room. She also became careful to avoid disagreement, especially in her family, because conflict now felt dangerous to her in a new way; ever since that last phone call with her son, even a minor argument carries the possibility of irreversible loss. At work, if a coworker starts talking about a recent highway pileup or shows a news clip on a phone, Meena abruptly walks the corridor or busies herself with checking doors, trying hard not to think. These efforts make sense to her as protection, yet they keep the crash poised just outside awareness, and when it does break through, it arrives with even greater force.

Her body has also stopped letting her believe the danger is over. On shift, seated behind the lobby desk watching the glass entrance and the street beyond, Meena scans constantly for signs that something bad is about to happen. A horn blast outside, the sight of dented cars from the parking garage cameras, even a cluster of mourners in dark clothing entering the building for a memorial service can make her heart race and her muscles lock. The physical jolt is so strong that the memory rushes in as if present, and once it does she becomes certain again that she is responsible, that a decent mother would have prevented this. Feeling so keyed up, she redoubles her efforts to stay away from reminders, to swallow thoughts before they fully form, and to steer clear of situations that might turn into conflict. But the more she lives braced for danger, the more she notices accident talk, damaged vehicles, and grief rituals everywhere around her. Already carrying a constant sense that catastrophe could break through at any moment, Meena finds that her mind turns ordinary cues into reminders before she has any chance to dismiss them; living at that pitch of alarm, a horn outside, dark clothing, or a traffic update can immediately register as another sign that the world is full of the same danger. Living at that level of alarm, ordinary sights and conversations are quickly reclassified as warnings; a news alert about traffic, a crumpled fender in the garage camera feed, or mourners in dark clothes all leap out at her because her mind is already searching for signs that another catastrophe is near.

Over time the pattern has narrowed her life. Her husband has become frustrated and lonely; he wants to visit their son’s grave and speak about him openly, while Meena shuts down or leaves the room. She hates that she cannot offer comfort to others in mourning, yet funerals and cemeteries feel unbearable, instantly charged with the vividness of the crash. Even at home she avoids television if there might be news footage of collisions, and if an image slips through, she spends the rest of the evening tense and watchful, unable to settle. On bad days she feels stripped of ordinary warmth, moving through routines without the emotions she used to trust, which only confirms her fear that she will never be normal again.

What finally brought Meena to seek help was an incident at work last month, when tenants gathered in the lobby discussing a fatal accident nearby. She felt her body surge, saw the crash in her mind as though it were unfolding in front of her, and had to retreat to the security office shaking and in tears. Afterward she was ashamed that she could not simply do her job. She has come to treatment frightened that if she lets herself remember, she will be swallowed by it, but also quietly hoping that someone might help her live in a world where every damaged car, every funeral, and every raised voice no longer feels like a fresh warning that she has failed beyond repair.
